title: Technology-facilitated violence is becoming a civic-space and public-participation constraint for women
source_unit: UN Women, Tipping point: The chilling escalation of violence against women in the public sphere in the age of AI
geography: Women in public life and public debate across 119 countries, with global survey and policy synthesis

observations.period: 2025 publication; global survey and synthesis across 119 countries

denominator.unit: countries represented in the global survey described by UN Women

public_sphere_targeting.value: women who speak publicly, report news, or defend human rights are targeted by online threats, abuse, and misinformation

participation_constraint.value: online attacks are framed as a threat to women’s ability to participate freely in public debate

civic_space_link.value: technology-facilitated violence is connected to shrinking civic space and backlash against women’s rights

public_actor_set.value: journalists, human-rights defenders, and other women speaking in public are visible target groups

observations.method: UN Women publication combining a global survey of women from 119 countries with analysis of technology-facilitated violence, public participation, and policy response.
observations.uncertainty: The source describes a global survey and public-space pattern; it is not a population prevalence estimate for every country, a platform incident census, or a causal estimate of participation loss.
observations.subgroup: Women journalists, activists, human-rights defenders, public officials, advocates, and others who speak or organize in public spaces.
observations.counterinterpretation: Online public participation can expand reach and solidarity; the finding concerns unequal exposure to abuse and retaliation, not an inevitable result of digital expression.

observations.period: 2025 publication; online-to-offline safety and well-being pathway

online_offline_spillover.value: harm that begins online can spill into offline intimidation, safety risks, and real-world harm

wellbeing_endpoint.value: online violence affects safety and well-being as well as public participation

visibility_cost.value: the threat can raise the personal and social cost of speaking, reporting, organizing, or defending rights
visibility_cost.unit: synthesis of the publication's participation pathway

boundary.value: digital abuse should not be treated as a separate or merely virtual harm category

observations.method: Policy and evidence synthesis linking online abuse to offline safety, well-being, and civic participation.
observations.uncertainty: The publication does not provide a universal conversion rate from online abuse to offline harm, and exposure and consequences vary by context, platform, identity, and access to support.
observations.subgroup: Women with public roles, women facing intersectional discrimination, journalists and defenders with visible public profiles, and people supporting or reporting abuse.
observations.counterinterpretation: Not every online attack produces offline harm, but the possibility of spillover is sufficient to make platform governance and public safety connected policy issues.

observations.period: 2025 publication; AI-enabled scaling and control problem

denominator.unit: UN Women AI and technology-facilitated violence assessment

content_generation.value: AI and other technologies make abusive content easier to create

control_difficulty.value: AI makes abusive content harder to control

governance_gap.value: the accelerating capacity to produce abuse increases pressure on platforms, regulators, and legal systems to detect, remove, prevent, and remedy it

power_endpoint.value: technology can alter who can speak safely and who is pushed out of public life

observations.method: UN Women analysis of technology-facilitated violence with specific attention to AI-enabled production and control challenges.
observations.uncertainty: The source identifies a direction of technological change but does not estimate future attack volumes, attribute all abuse to AI, or evaluate the effectiveness of specific detection systems.
observations.subgroup: Women public figures, journalists, activists, human-rights defenders, platforms, regulators, law-enforcement and support organizations.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI can also support moderation, documentation, and safety tools; governance quality determines whether it amplifies abuse or helps reduce it.

observations.period: 2025 publication; recommended public, legal, and platform response

platform_route.value: digital platforms should become safer and more capable of responding to technology-facilitated violence

legal_route.value: legal protections should be strengthened to address online and technology-facilitated abuse

support_route.value: women experiencing abuse need support to remain safe and participate in public life

accountability_boundary.value: response requires coordination among platforms, governments, civil society, and affected women rather than treating abuse as an individual resilience problem

observations.method: UN Women policy recommendations grounded in the publication's global survey and public-participation analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The recommendations are not an implementation audit or evaluation of a particular law, platform intervention, or support service.
observations.subgroup: Women affected by online violence, platforms, regulators, justice systems, civil-society organizations, and public institutions responsible for civic-space protection.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stronger rules can improve safety, but overbroad moderation or weak due process can also restrict legitimate speech; remedy and proportionality remain important.

related_sources.claim: Related UN Women publication on gender-inclusive digital public infrastructure and safeguards.
UN Women publication catalogue and related technology-facilitated violence resources.

boundary: This record adds a civic-space and platform-governance route across online violence, offline safety, AI-enabled abuse, women’s public participation, legal protection, platform accountability, and support. It uses a UN Women global survey and policy synthesis, not a country-by-country prevalence census, raw platform incident logs, respondent-level harm histories, causal participation estimates, or proof that every moderation or legal response is effective and proportionate.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UN Women publication listing and search-visible publication summary reviewed for the 119-country survey scope, public-sphere targeting, online-to-offline spillover, AI escalation, civic-space link, and response recommendations.
